# Mahāmālukya Sutta (MN 64 (PTS MN i 432))

**ID:** MN 64 (PTS MN i 432)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāmālukya Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Longer Discourse With Māluṅkya
**PTS:** MN i 432
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn64
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāmālukya Sutta* (MN 64) is a discourse of the Majjhimanikāya delivered by the Buddha concerning the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañc' orambhāgiyāni samyojanāni*) [Radich 2007; Park 2007]. In response to an answer by the monk Māluṅkyāputta, the Buddha observes that an infant lying prone lacks explicit notions such as identity view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt, rule-adherence, sensual desire, or malevolence, yet still harbors the underlying latent tendencies (*anusaya*) for them [Edelglass and Garfield 2009; Johansson 1979; Radich 2007]. The sutta thus underscores that early Buddhism does not view the mind of a newborn as a *tabula rasa* [Edelglass and Garfield 2009; Sujato 2011].

To eradicate these fetters, the Buddha sets forth a meditative path wherein a practitioner enters the four jhānas or the immaterial attainments and contemplates their constituent factors (*dhammā*) as impermanent, conditioned, suffering, and non-self, ultimately turning the mind toward the "deathless element" (*amatadhātu*) [Law 1931; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Shulman 2014; Wen 2011]. Scholars note that unlike later commentarial models where insight occurs after emerging from absorption, MN 64 depicts discriminating insight as realized directly within or upon these high states of concentration [Vetter 1988; Hung 2010; Wen 2011]. Within modern chronology, G. C. Pande considered the discourse to be relatively late among canonical treatments of *amata* [Radich 2007].

SuttaCentral records full parallels in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 205), a Sanskrit fragment in the Schøyen/Turfan collections (SHT sutta 57), and an Abhidharma parallel in T 1537.15, alongside close canonical counterparts in MN 52 (*Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta*), AN 9.36 (*Jhāna Sutta*), and AN 11.16 [SuttaCentral; Hung 2010; Shulman 2014; Wen 2011]. DharmaNexus automatically aligns MN 64 with MĀ 205 (T 26.56) and confirms extensive Pali-internal text reuse with AN 9 (especially AN 9.36, sharing over 17,000 characters), AN 11 (AN 11.16), and the *Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta* (SN 46) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns the text with the Tibetan translation of Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D 4094), reflecting Vasubandhu's and later scholiasts' reliance on the sutta's analysis of fetters and latent seeds [Park 2007; DharmaNexus].
